title: Working with Class Instances
objective: Give a property a default value in the constructor, then update it both directly and through a method.

sourceAlignment.title: JavaScript Crash Course
sourceAlignment.author: Nick Morgan
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: Not every property needs to come from a constructor argument. Inside the constructor you can also assign a fixed starting value directly, giving every new instance the same default state before anything else happens to it.

Once an instance exists, you can change its properties in two ways. The direct way reaches straight into the instance with dot notation, like instance.property = newValue. This works, but it bypasses whatever logic a method might otherwise run.

The second way is to call a method that updates the property on the instance's behalf. A method can check the new value, combine it with the current one, or update more than one property at once — plain direct assignment can't do any of that.
explanation.rule: Give a property a default value inside the constructor, then update it either directly with dot notation or through a method that changes it for you.

examples.title: A Default Value, Then Two Ways to Change It
examples.note: energy comes from a fixed default (100), not an argument. It's then changed directly with bot.energy = 50, and again through the charge() method, ending at 60.

checks.question: class Widget { constructor() { this.count = 0; } } — where does the value of count come from?
options: A constructor argument the caller must supply.
A fixed default assigned directly inside the constructor.
It's undefined until set some other way.

feedback.correct: Correct — this.count = 0 assigns a fixed default value directly, with no argument involved.
feedback.incorrect: There's no parameter here — this.count = 0 is a fixed default the constructor assigns to every new instance.

assignment.title: Training Dummy
assignment.brief: Write a TrainingDummy class whose hitCount starts at 0 by default (not from an argument), with a hit() method that increments hitCount by 1. Then write runTraining() that creates one dummy, calls hit() twice, sets hitCount directly to 10, calls hit() once more, and logs the final hitCount.
requirements: Define class TrainingDummy with a constructor() that sets this.hitCount = 0 (no constructor argument).
Define a hit() method that increments this.hitCount by 1.
Define runTraining() that creates a TrainingDummy, calls hit() twice, sets hitCount directly to 10, calls hit() once more, then logs hitCount.
assignment.outputCheckLabel: runTraining() logs 11 (10 set directly, then one more hit)

hints: The constructor takes no argument for hitCount — just assign this.hitCount = 0 directly.
dummy.hitCount = 10 changes the property directly, bypassing hit() entirely.
After hitting twice (irrelevant once overwritten), setting to 10, then hitting once more: 10 + 1 = 11.
